evidence_quotes.quote: Nuestro análisis estuvo basado en observación participante, conversaciones informales, entrevistas en profundidad, historias de vida, recorridos etnográficos y cartografía social. El proyecto tuvo una duración de dieciocho meses, desde mayo de 2013 hasta octubre de 2014.

En el caso del distrito de riego de María La Baja, cedido en concesión a la Asociación de Usuarios de María La Baja (Usomaría), el cambio en la forma de propiedad y administración del distrito de riego relegó a muchos pobladores locales que no contaban con títulos de propiedad ni con los recursos necesarios para poder hacer parte de la asociación.

Incluso, las parcelas productivas, pequeñas extensiones de tierra adquiridas por pobladores locales bajo figuras comunitarias, no fueron (ni son) tenidas en cuenta por las políticas estatales, ya que sin títulos de propiedad individual no pueden ser incluidas para concesiones de agua.

El despojo del agua para uso doméstico, a pesar de ser una realidad apabullante para gran número de pobladores rurales en la región, se forja a través del día a día. El acceso a este recurso depende en buena medida de dónde logren recoger agua para luego llevarla en “pimpinas” (galones de plástico) hasta sus hogares.

Éste es también el caso de pobladores que habitan en las inmediaciones de la planta de tratamiento de María La Baja, quienes para poder tener acceso a agua para beber y cocinar deben pedir a los funcionarios de la planta que “les hagan el favor” de llenarles sus tanques y jarras con el líquido tratado

A pesar de que esta población está ubicada muy cerca de la planta de tratamiento de agua, que hace parte del distrito de riego y desde donde se distribuye el agua tratada al casco urbano de María La Baja, ninguna de las casas cuenta con acueducto ni alcantarillado.

criterion_notes.c1: Although much of the paper addresses agrarian land grabbing and agricultural irrigation, a dedicated empirical section ('Las geografías desiguales del acceso al agua', PDF pp. 8-9 / pp. 114-115) explicitly examines rural household and community access to domestic and potable water ('agua para uso doméstico', 'agua potable', 'agua para beber y cocinar'), lack of piped water and sewerage connections ('ninguna de las casas cuenta con acueducto ni alcantarillado') in settlements adjacent to the María La Baja water treatment plant, and loss of communal water sources ('jagüeyes' and reservoirs).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading (though somewhat borderline because the primary institutional vehicle is a privatized irrigation/water district rather than a standalone municipal utility). Under the plain reading, it examines state water privatization, property-titling law (Ley 1182 de 2008), and water governance. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it specifically analyzes: (1) ownership/concession transfer of public water infrastructure (the María La Baja district, which also encompasses the water treatment plant supplying the urban core) to a private users' association (Usomaría); (2) tenure/documentation rules requiring individual property titles ('títulos de propiedad individual') for water concessions and association membership, excluding untitled rural inhabitants and collective landholdings ('parcelas productivas'); (3) beneficiary eligibility and payment rules excluding surrounding rural households as official beneficiaries and restricting canal water to paying agroindustrial users; (4) frontline discretion at the water treatment plant where excluded nearby residents must ask plant officials as a 'favor' to fill jugs with treated drinking water; and (5) private property titling/enclosure of communal water ponds ('jagüeyes').
criterion_notes.c3: Collaborative qualitative ethnographic study conducted over 18 months (May 2013 to October 2014) across six field visits in Montes de María, based on participant observation, informal conversations, in-depth interviews (16 cited interviewees listed on p. 119), life histories, ethnographic walks, and social cartography. Per protocol rules, qualitative socio-legal/empirical studies are eligible for the mechanism synthesis without quantitative effect estimates.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete qualitative household and community water access and exclusion outcomes: lack of aqueduct and sewerage connections despite proximity to the water treatment plant supplying urban María La Baja, exclusion from official beneficiary status, dependence on informal favors from treatment plant staff for drinking/cooking water, reliance on hauling contaminated or stagnant canal water in plastic jugs ('pimpinas') or rainwater, seasonal scarcity when canal gates are controlled for oil palm, and loss of access to enclosed communal 'jagüeyes'.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (rural campesino, Afro-descendant, and Indigenous households and communities in Montes de María municipalities including María La Baja, Ovejas, San Onofre, and El Carmen de Bolívar), legal/institutional exposures, domestic/community water access outcomes, and qualitative ethnographic case-study design are clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Spanish (with English, Spanish, and Portuguese abstracts). Under Inclusion Criterion 10, non-English/Portuguese/Dutch studies are eligible when translation from the accessible full text is feasible and the study is potentially important for the mechanism synthesis; translation method/translator should be logged in extraction_note during data extraction.

study_design: Qualitative collaborative ethnographic case study (participant observation, in-depth interviews, life histories, ethnographic walks, and social cartography)
population_and_sample: Rural campesino, Afro-descendant, and Indigenous households and communities (linked to the Organización de Poblaciones Desplazadas and grassroots groups) across municipalities in Montes de María, Colombia (especially María La Baja, Ovejas, San Onofre, and El Carmen de Bolívar); 18-month ethnographic fieldwork with 16 named interview records listed
exposure: Privatization/concession of public water infrastructure (María La Baja water/irrigation district, including its water treatment plant) to a private users' association (Usomaría), individual land-title requirements excluding untitled households and communal parcels from water concessions, beneficiary/payment rules favoring agroindustrial oil palm, private property titling/enclosure of communal water ponds (jagüeyes), and discretionary gatekeeping by water treatment plant staff
outcome: Household and community exclusion from potable and domestic water service (lack of aqueduct and sewerage connections in settlements adjacent to the water treatment plant, exclusion as official beneficiaries, reliance on informal staff favors for treated drinking/cooking water, hauling contaminated canal water in plastic jugs, seasonal water scarcity, and loss of access to enclosed communal water sources)
rationale: This 18-month collaborative ethnographic study in Montes de María, Colombia satisfies all inclusion criteria for the qualitative mechanism synthesis. While framed around agrarian land and water grabbing, Section 'Las geografías desiguales del acceso al agua' (pp. 114-115) directly examines rural household and community exclusion from domestic and potable water, including lack of aqueduct/sewerage connections next to the district's urban-serving water treatment plant. It identifies concrete rule-type legal/institutional mechanisms under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2: concession of public water infrastructure to a private association (Usomaría), individual land-title documentation requirements for water concessions that exclude untitled residents and collective parcels, payment and crop-eligibility rules excluding surrounding rural settlements as official beneficiaries, private titling/enclosure of communal water sources ('jagüeyes'), and reliance on frontline staff discretion ('hacer el favor') at the treatment plant to obtain drinking water. Full text is in Spanish and directly translatable per Inclusion Criterion 10.
